assignment: When people ask for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. Explain why seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice. Use specific details and examples in your response.
essay_1:
Why One Opinion Is Not Enough

Last year my cousin got offered a job in a different city and she didn't know if she should take it. The first person she asked was her dad. He told her to stay because the pay was only a little bit more and she would be far away from the family. If she stopped right there she probably would of said no. But she kept asking people, and three other people told her stuff that changed her mind. I think this shows that asking more than one person helps you make a better choice. One person only knows part of the story, people have there own feelings mixed in, and hearing different opinions helps you figure out what you really want.

My first reason is that nobody knows everything. My cousin's dad knew about money and about family, but he never worked in the kind of job she does. So then she talked to a lady she used to work with who had moved for a job before. That lady said the new company was really good at training people and after two years there she could get way better jobs. She also asked a friend who lives in that city. Her friend told her how much rent really costs and which neighborhoods are too far to drive from. None of them had the whole answer by themself. But when you put it all together she knew about the pay and the career and what living there would be like. Her dad could not of told her all that even if he wanted to.

My second reason is that people's feelings get into there advice. Her dad loves her and he didn't want her to move away. So of course he said stay, even though he thought he was just being practical. I don't think that is lying. It's just how people are. It's kind of like with doctors. A doctor who does surgery all day might tell you to get surgery faster then another doctor would, and that's why people get a second opinion before a big operation. If you only ask one person you can't tell what part of the advice is about you and what part is really about them. If you ask a few people it is easier to notice because the other people don't have that same feeling.

My third reason is that listening to other people teaches you about yourself. When her friend was telling her about the city, my cousin noticed she was getting excited. When her dad was listing reasons to stay, she noticed she kept trying to think of ways he was wrong. Nobody told her that, she just saw how she was reacting. Also it helps when people disagree. If everybody says the same thing then you can feel pretty sure about it. If they say different things, then you know which part is the hard part and you can think about that part the most.

I'm not saying you should just count votes and do what most people say. That would be dumb because then it's not even your choice. And if you ask too many people it gets confusing. It is still your choice in the end because you are the one who has to live with it. My cousin took the job and she decided that herself. But she knew a lot more then she did after just talking to her dad, and that is why you should ask more than one person before you make a big choice.
essay_2:
Why One Opinion Is Not Enough

Last year my cousin had to decide if she should take a job in another city. The first person she asked was her dad. He told her to stay, because the pay was only a little higher and she would be far from the family. If she had stopped there, she probably would have said no to the job. Instead she kept asking, and what she heard from three other people changed her mind. I think her story shows why you should talk to more than one person before you make a big choice. Each person only knows part of the picture, each person has their own feelings mixed in, and hearing a few different views shows you what you actually want.

The first reason is that no one knows everything. My cousin's dad knew about money and family, but he had never worked in her kind of job. A person she used to work with had made the same kind of move, and she said the new company trains people well. She said two years there would open doors the old job never would. Then a friend who lives in that city told her what rent costs and which neighborhoods are close to the office. None of them had the whole answer. When you put all three together, she knew about the pay, the career, and what every day would be like. One person could not have told her all of that.

The second reason is that advice comes with the feelings of the person giving it. Her dad did not want her to move away, so of course he said to stay. He was not lying. He thought he was just being practical. That is how people are. It is the same with doctors. A doctor who does surgery all day might suggest surgery faster, and that is why people get a second opinion before an operation. If you ask only one person, you can't tell which part of the advice is about you and which part is about them. If you ask a few people, you can see it, because the others do not feel the same way.

The third reason is one I did not think of at first. Listening to other people teaches you about yourself. When my cousin's friend talked about the city, she noticed she was really excited. When her dad listed reasons to stay, she noticed she kept looking for ways to answer him. Nobody could have told her that. She had to hear both sides to find out. It also helps when people do not agree. If everyone says the same thing, you can feel pretty sure. If they say different things, you know which question you need to think about the most.

Asking more people does not mean you count votes. The choice still belongs to the person who has to live with it. My cousin took the job. She misses her family sometimes, but she is happy there now. She chose it herself, and she knew a lot more than she did after the first talk. That is why I believe you should ask around before a big decision. It takes more time, and it gave my cousin a better choice in the end.
